title: Text Completion: two and three blanks
lines: ## What you see on screen

A multi-blank text completion shows a passage of one to five sentences with two or three gaps, marked (i), (ii) and (iii). Under the passage there is a separate column of three choices for each blank. You click one choice in every column.

The scoring rule changes everything: you get credit only if every blank is right. Two correct blanks out of three earn exactly the same as zero. That means you must check how the blanks fit together, not just whether each choice sounds good alone.
## Why the blanks interlock

In a well-built item the blanks depend on each other. The meaning of blank (i) changes the logic of the sentence around blank (ii), and so on. Each column usually contains one choice that looks attractive in isolation but contradicts the choice another blank requires. The question tests logical structure, tone and idiom across the whole passage, so vocabulary alone is not enough.
## The method step by step
- Step 1: Read the entire passage first, ignoring all choices. Get the overall story: what is being described, and does the writer approve, disapprove or report neutrally?
- Step 2: Pick the easiest blank, not the first one. The easiest blank is the one with the strongest clue nearby. Often this is blank (ii) or (iii).
- Step 3: Predict a word for that blank and choose it from its column.
- Step 4: Plug that choice into the passage. It now acts as a new clue for the remaining blanks.
- Step 5: Predict and choose the next blank, then the last one.
- Step 6: Reread the whole passage with all your choices in place. It must read as one coherent thought. If it does not, the weak link is usually the blank you were least sure of.
## Worked example: two blanks

> Early reviewers found the composer's late quartets (i) ____, complaining that the music wandered without direction. Later scholars, however, discovered in them a (ii) ____ design: every theme returns, transformed, in the final movement.
> Blank (i) choices: incoherent, sublime, conventional. Blank (ii) choices: haphazard, meticulous, derivative.

> Start with blank (i), because its clue is right beside it: "complaining that the music wandered without direction". Prediction: aimless. "Incoherent" fits; "sublime" (awe-inspiring) has the wrong charge; "conventional" is negative-sounding but describes predictability, not wandering.

> Blank (ii): "however" signals a turn from the early complaint, and the colon tells us the design is one where every theme returns. Prediction: carefully planned. "Meticulous" fits. "Haphazard" agrees with the early reviewers, which ignores "however". "Derivative" (borrowed from others) is negative and off-topic.
Notice the interlock: anyone who chose "sublime" for blank (i) would have no logical reason for the "however" that follows.
## Worked example: three blanks, starting in the middle

> The economist's forecast was initially greeted with (i) ____; few colleagues believed that so small a change in interest rates could (ii) ____ such a large shift in spending. When the shift arrived on schedule, her critics were forced to (iii) ____ their earlier doubts.
> Blank (i): enthusiasm, skepticism, indifference. Blank (ii): precipitate, forestall, obscure. Blank (iii): reiterate, recant, conceal.

> The easiest blank is (i), whose clue is in the same sentence: "few colleagues believed". Prediction: doubt. "Skepticism" fits. "Indifference" is the trap, since doubting is not the same as not caring.
> Blank (ii): the colleagues doubted that a small change could cause a large shift. Prediction: cause. "Precipitate" (bring about suddenly) fits. "Forestall" (prevent) is the reverse.

> Blank (iii): the shift arrived as predicted, so the critics were proved wrong. Prediction: take back. "Recant" (formally withdraw a statement) fits. "Reiterate" (repeat) is the opposite; "conceal" might be tempting if you imagine embarrassed critics, but the sentence says they were "forced", which suits a public withdrawal.
## Worked example: when the easiest blank is last
> Although the museum's new wing was praised for its (i) ____, many visitors found that its very (ii) ____ made it hard to navigate; the director admitted that the design had perhaps been (iii) ____.
> Blank (i): austerity, novelty, accessibility. Blank (ii): inventiveness, plainness, convenience. Blank (iii): overly ambitious, insufficiently daring, carelessly built.

> Blank (i) has almost no clue by itself. Start with (iii): the director admits a design fault linked to being hard to navigate. "Overly ambitious" fits a design that tried too much; "insufficiently daring" is the reverse; "carelessly built" is about construction, not design.

> Now blank (ii): the quality that made it hard to navigate, and the word "very" means the praised quality and the problem are the same thing. An ambitious design is "inventive". So blank (i) must be its partner, "novelty", since the wing was praised for exactly what caused the problem.

> Check "accessibility": praising accessibility and then calling the wing hard to navigate is a contradiction, not the irony "very" signals. "Austerity" would pair with "plainness", but a plain design is not "overly ambitious". That pair fails at blank (iii), which is exactly how interlocking traps work.
## Tone and idiom

Multi-blank items often turn on tone. A passage that describes a writer "with grudging admiration" needs words that are positive but restrained, not glowing. Watch also for set phrases: one "pays tribute to" something, "falls short of" a standard, is "at odds with" a view, and something can be "anything but" simple (meaning very complicated). When a choice creates an awkward or unidiomatic phrase, be suspicious.
## Traps the GRE sets
! The lone-wolf trap: a choice that fits its own blank perfectly but clashes with the rest of the passage. The fix is the final reread with all choices in place.

! The first-blank trap: starting with blank (i) only because it comes first. If its clue is weak, you will guess, and that guess will steer the other blanks wrong. Start where the evidence is strongest.
! The partial-credit illusion: there is none. If you are certain of two blanks and unsure of the third, that third blank decides the whole item, so give it the extra 20 seconds.

! The pairing trap: the test likes to offer a matched pair of wrong answers across two columns (such as "austerity" and "plainness") that agree with each other but not with a third clue. Agreement between two blanks is necessary but not sufficient.
! The reversal trap: words such as "however", "yet" and "paradoxically" may sit between two blanks. Check whether the second blank should agree with or oppose the first.
## Timing

Budget about one minute for a two-blank item and about 1.5 minutes for a three-blank item. Across a section, this averages out to roughly one minute per verbal question when combined with faster one-blank and sentence equivalence items. If a three-blank passage still makes no sense after two minutes, choose the most consistent set you have, mark it, and return later with fresh eyes.
## Quick checklist
- Did I read the whole passage before looking at any choices?
- Which blank has the strongest clue? Start there.
- Did each new choice act as a clue for the next blank?
- Does the passage read as one logical, consistent thought with all choices in place?
